title: SIEM export — tenant-aware routing, customer-side redaction profiles, and SLA negotiation
content:
Purpose and scope
This working doc defines an approach for SIEM export connectors that supports:
- per-tenant routing (tenant-aware delivery with optional customer-managed endpoints)
- customer-side transformation and redaction profiles so customers can enforce privacy requirements before leaving Redwood systems
- an SLA negotiation matrix and operational acceptance criteria for Dedicated/Private customers integrating Splunk, Datadog, and Azure Sentinel

This doc is intentionally practical: it captures minimum required fields, example payload mappings, redaction rule semantics, error modes, and acceptance tests for onboarding. It complements the existing SIEM connector specs by focusing on tenant routing and customer-side controls.

Background and motivations
Customers increasingly ask for two capabilities that complicate a single flat export pipeline: (1) the ability to route different tenants to different downstream SIEM targets (multi-tenant exporters with per-tenant mapping) and (2) the desire to apply redaction/transformations owned by the customer before events leave Redwood (for compliance/regulatory needs). Supporting these safely requires:
- clear contract (schema) between Redwood and downstream SIEMs
- idempotency and ordering guarantees per tenant
- RBAC-v2 considerations for who can change routing or redaction profiles
- audit evidence hooks so each transformation is itself auditable

Key definitions
- Tenant: logical customer space (could be org, team, or account).
- Delivery target: a single SIEM ingestion endpoint (e.g., Splunk HEC token+URL, Datadog Logs API key+URL, Azure Event Hub / Log Analytics workspace).
- Redaction profile: named set of transformation rules (regex, json-path, pseudonymization) applied to events before delivery. Profiles are versioned.
- Proof bundle: minimal evidence package stored in Redwood (hash of original event, transformation id, operator id, timestamp) sufficient for post-fact audit.

Minimum required event schema (Redwood canonical audit-record)
Every exported event must at least contain these fields. Downstream mappings map them to SIEM-specific fields.
- event_id: string (UUID v4)
- tenant_id: string
- timestamp_utc: RFC3339
- source: string (service/component sending the event)
- event_type: string (e.g., infra.alert, api.request, rbac.change)
- severity: string (INFO|WARN|ERROR|CRITICAL)
- payload: JSON string or object
- redaction_profile_applied: string|null
- original_hash: hex (sha256 of raw payload before redaction)
- processed_at: RFC3339
- processed_by: string (system or operator id)

Per-tenant routing model
Customers may supply one of the following routing modes per tenant:
1) Managed Redwood routing: Redwood hosts connectors and credentials; customer picks a delivery target profile from a UI and Redwood manages credentials.
2) Customer-managed endpoint: customer provides a stable URL and auth token/certificate; Redwood pushes events to that endpoint and does not store the secret beyond an encrypted runtime store.
3) Hybrid proxy: Redwood forwards events to a customer proxy inside their VPC; the proxy pulls from Redwood over a secure channel. Useful for air-gapped environments.

Routing config fields (example)
- tenant_id
- delivery_mode: managed | customer_managed | hybrid_proxy
- target_type: splunk | datadog | sentinel | custom_http
- target_uri: string (only for customer_managed/hybrid_proxy)
- auth_mode: hec_token | api_key | mTLS | none
- redaction_profile: profile_name|null
- fallback_target: optional (another delivery target id)
- max_unacked_bytes: integer (backpressure)

Redaction profile design and semantics
Goals: flexible but auditable. Profiles support 3 transformation types: redaction (remove field/value), pseudonymization (consistent hash with salt), and truncate (limit length). Rules are applied to named JSON paths; when a value is removed we replace with the token "[REDACTED]" and record in the proof bundle.

Profile components:
- profile_id (string), version (semver-like), owner (tenant or org), created_at, rules (ordered list)
- rule: id, op (redact|pseudonymize|truncate|regex-mask), path (json-path), pattern (optional regex), salt_id (for pseudonymize), note

Important semantics:
- Rules execute in declared order; later rules can refer to previously pseudonymized values.
- Pseudonymization must be reversible only for allowed support workflows; reversible keys are stored in customer KMS if requested (Private/Dedicated).
- Proof bundle includes rule version, rule ids applied, and original_hash; this bundle is stored with an HMAC using a per-tenant signing key.

SIEM-specific mapping notes and examples
Splunk HEC (JSON events)
- Redwood canonical fields map as: event_id -> event_id, sourcetype -> redwood:rr-audit, host -> tenant_id, time -> timestamp_utc (epoch), fields -> event_type, severity-> severity, _raw -> payload (stringified)
- Recommended HEC payload example (JSON): {"event": {..}, "host": "tenant-123", "sourcetype": "redwood:rr-audit", "index": "customer_index"}
- When customer expects metadata extraction, Redwood will populate dedicated top-level fields (e.g., user_id, session_id) rather than rely on HEC regex.

Datadog Logs API
- Map timestamp to timestamp, attributes flattened to top-level tags, and provide "redwood_event_id" as a dedicated attribute.
- For high-throughput tenants, prefer Datadog batch endpoint with 10k events per request with max payload size 10MB per batch. Redwood will auto-batch respecting per-tenant rate limits.

Azure Sentinel (Log Analytics / Event Hub)
- Support both ingestion via Event Hub and direct Log Analytics HTTP Data Collector API.
- Map Redwood fields into a custom table schema; ensure timestamp field is named TimeGenerated for KQL compatibility.

Operational behaviors and edge cases
Backpressure and retries
- Per-tenant unacked bytes and event queue length thresholds are enforced.
- Retry policy: exponential backoff with jitter, three retries by default for transient errors (5xx/timeout). For 4xx (auth failures) do not retry; instead mark tenant state as "credential-error" and alert the customer.
- For managed targets, Redwood initiates credential rotation per schedule; rotation failures transition tenant to "pending-credentials" with a monitored escalation.

Idempotency and ordering
- Each event contains event_id and original_hash. Downstream connectors will include event_id in delivery metadata and implement at-least-once delivery. Redwood will retain a short window (72h) for de-duplication hints; longer deduplication must be managed by the customer SIEM.
- Ordering is per-tenant best-effort; strict ordering requires the tenant to opt into a single-partition delivery mode and accept throughput trade-offs.

Auditability and evidence automation hooks
- Every transformation run produces a proof bundle: {event_id, original_hash, redaction_profile: name@version, rules_applied: [ids], transformed_hash, processed_by, processed_at, signature}. This bundle is stored in the tenant audit log and referenced in the exported event as a pointer (S3 URL or internal id), not embedded, to avoid duplication.
- Evidence automation: When a compliance workflow requires a proof artifact (e.g., for subject access requests), operators can redeem proof bundles via an audit API that returns a time-limited signed package.

RBAC-v2 controls (who can change what)
- Roles and permissions needed:
  - tenant.admin: can change routing and redaction profiles, view proof bundles
  - tenant.audit: can view exported events and proof bundles but cannot edit routing
  - platform.security: can view all tenant configs for incident response but cannot export proof bundles without tenant consent (policy)
- UI actions that mutate routing or profiles must annotate the change with a Jira ticket id or approval record when the tenant is in a regulated plan; this action is recorded as an audit event emitted through the same SIEM pipeline.

Onboarding checklist for customers (minimum acceptance criteria)
1) Customer fills routing template (delivery_mode, target_uri, auth, desired index/table, retention expectations)
2) Customer provides test credentials (for customer_managed) or confirms managed delivery selection
3) Redwood side smoke tests: 1k synthetic events, check ingestion, field mapping correctness, and proof bundle generation
4) Latency/throughput acceptance: define SLOs (p50/p95/p99) and max daily ingest rate; for Dedicated customers measure on a staging GPU pool if relevant
5) Failure mode test: simulate transient 5xx, auth failures, and long-tail backpressure; ensure alerts and fallback_target behavior are validated

Security and data residency notes
- For customers requiring regional residency, delivery targets must be inside requested region and key material (for pseudonymization reversible keys) stored in regional KMS when requested.
- All secrets are stored encrypted with a platform KMS; for Private deployments we require integration with customer KMS/HSM for reversible transformations.

Testing and acceptance criteria (QA)
- Unit tests for rule engine (coverage for regex, pseudonymize salt, truncate)
- Integration tests with mocked Splunk/Datadog/Sentinel endpoints verifying: preserved event_id, correct field mapping, proof bundle pointer included, redaction semantics (assert original_hash != transformed_hash when modification applied)
- Load test: per-tenant 10k eps sustained for 1 hour for high-volume customers with observed error rate < 0.1%

Failure & escalation playbook (operations)
- Credential failure: alert to tenant and SE, set tenant state to credential-error, pause exports for that tenant after 30 min failed attempts.
- Delivery degradation: if per-tenant error rate > 1% for 15 min escalate to on-call SRE. Use fallback_target if configured.
- Proof-bundle storage failure: do not proceed with export until proof bundle store can accept writes; if transient, keep events queued for up to 6h then use fallback_policy (deliver without proof if tenant consents)

Data retention and purge
- Default proof bundle retention: 1 year; configurable per-tenant up to 7 years for regulated customers.
- Exported events retention in Redwood: default 30 days for logs; for longer retention customers use Dedicated or Private and follow contract terms.

Open questions and decisions needed (for next RFC)
- Reversible pseudonymization key custody: default platform-managed vs customer-managed by plan tier?
- Default deduplication window: 72h is proposed — is that sufficient for cross-region replays?
- Should proof bundles be encrypted with tenant keys by default? Pros: stronger isolation. Cons: more complex rotation semantics.

Appendix: small examples
1) Example redaction rule (json)
- id: r-ssn-mask-1
- op: regex-mask
- path: $.payload.user.ssn
- pattern: "(\\d{3})-(\\d{2})-(\\d{4})"
- note: mask all but last 4 digits

2) Sample Splunk HEC outgoing event (post-redaction)
{
  "time": 1700000000.0,
  "host": "tenant-123",
  "sourcetype": "redwood:rr-audit",
  "event": {"event_id": "...", "event_type": "api.request", "severity": "INFO", "payload": "{\"user\":{\"id\":\"u-1\", \"ssn\":\"[REDACTED]\"}}", "redaction_profile_applied": "pii-mask-v2"},
  "index": "tenant_logs"
}

Next steps
- Review with SRE and product-hosted-api to align on batching and retry defaults (target: 2025-11-20)
- Decide on key-custody default (platform vs customer) and add to contract templates
- Create a lightweight UI draft for tenant routing and profile selection (product/UX ticket)

Notes to reviewers
This file is intended as a working document; please comment inline (Confluence linked) or drop design notes into JIRA-SIEM-112. We should avoid duplicating field-level mapping docs — instead link to the canonical field mapping appendix once finalized.
